lessons.title: കുട്ടി (kuṭṭi) — "child, kid," the general word before the specific ones
lessons.gloss: child, kid — the general word, native Dravidian, before Malayalam narrows to son or daughter

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Suhṛttŭ named someone you choose. This chapter turns to someone you don't — the people a family is built around.
ഇത് എന്റെ കുട്ടിയാണ്. — ithu ente kuṭṭiyāṇŭ. — "This is my child."
കുട്ടി (kuṭṭi) is the general word — any child, before you say whose son or daughter.

കുട്ടി is native Dravidian, matching Tamil's குட்டி (kuṭṭi) closely. Both languages let the same word cover two things: a human child, and the young of an animal — a പൂച്ചക്കുട്ടി (pūccakkuṭṭi) is a kitten, built on പൂച്ച, "cat," met earlier in this book, the same way kuṭṭi attaches to any animal name for its young. English does something similar with "kid," which covers both a child and a baby goat — one small word, carrying the same double duty in two unrelated language families.

segments.source: [PAUSE 1s]

segments.text: Say "this is my child." (Ithu ente kuṭṭiyāṇŭ.) What two things can kuṭṭi mean? (A human child, or the young of an animal — like pūccakkuṭṭi, kitten.) Which English word carries the very same double duty? (Kid.) Name the six family people-words once more, and the group word none of them supplied. (Acchan, amma, cēṭṭan, aniyan, cēcci, aniyatti — and kuṭumbaṁ.)

lessons.title: മകൻ (makan) — "son," a word Tamil hardly changed at all
lessons.gloss: son — Proto-Dravidian, closely matching Tamil, where Kannada softened the same root

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Kuṭṭi was the general word. Now the two specific ones — starting with the son.
ഇത് എന്റെ മകനാണ്. — ithu ente makanāṇŭ. — "This is my son."

മകൻ continues Proto-Dravidian makan, "son." Tamil keeps almost the identical shape, மகன் (makan) — same consonants, same vowels, same final -n. Kannada moved further: the -k- between vowels softened to -g-, and the final -n dropped, giving ಮಗ (maga). So on this word it is Malayalam and Tamil that hold the older, more conservative shape, and Kannada that innovated — the same closeness the very first greetings already showed in nandi, athe, illa and śari, this time in a family word rather than a greeting.

segments.source: [PAUSE 1s]

segments.instruction: "ithu ente makanāṇŭ" — this is my son
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "ithu ente makanāṇŭ" — this is my son]
[YOU SAY: the two cousins — "makan" (Malayalam, Tamil) … "maga" (Kannada)]
[YOU SAY: general then specific — "kuṭṭi … makan"]

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the friend-word, once more — "suhṛttŭ" — su plus hṛd]

segments.text: Say "this is my son." (Ithu ente makanāṇŭ.) Which sister keeps almost the identical word? (Tamil — makan.) What did Kannada change? (Softened -k- to -g- and dropped the final -n, giving maga.) What does suhṛttŭ literally mean? ("Good-heart" — su plus hṛd.)

lessons.title: മകൾ (makaḷ) — "daughter," the closest match yet
lessons.gloss: daughter — identical to Tamil's own word, sound for sound, closer even than the son-word

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Makan matched Tamil closely. Its pair matches even closer — and gives you a reason to ask an old question again.
ഇത് എന്റെ മകളാണ്. — ithu ente makaḷāṇŭ. — "This is my daughter."

മകൾ continues Proto-Dravidian makaḷ, "daughter." Tamil's மகள் (makaḷ) is not just close — it is identical, sound for sound. Kannada shows the same softening you just met in maga: ಮಗಳು (magaḷu), -k- to -g-, plus a closing -u. So where makan/makan was already a close match, makaḷ/makaḷ is the closer one still — two sisters holding one Proto-Dravidian root letter for letter, four thousand years and a script apart.

Now that you have a son and a daughter, the age question comes back with someone new to ask it about: ninṟe makanŭ ethra vayassuṇṭŭ? — "how old is your son?" — the same dative-subject-plus-uṇṭŭ shape, unchanged.

segments.text: Say "this is my daughter." (Ithu ente makaḷāṇŭ.) How closely does Tamil match this word, compared with makan? (Even closer — makaḷ is identical sound for sound, where makan only nearly matched.) Ask "how old is your son?" using the age question's shape. (Ninṟe makanŭ ethra vayassuṇṭŭ? — "to your son, how much age exists?") What is the general word for a child, before makan or makaḷ? (കുട്ടി, kuṭṭi.)
